chapters.title: Call to order, land acknowledgement and roll call
chapters.summary: Chair Mike Edgington called the March 23, 2026 regular meeting to order at 7 p.m., Bryan Burnett read the land acknowledgement, and roll call found all five supervisors present.
bullets: The chair read the conduct announcement asking the public to raise hands and direct comments to the board.

chapters.title: Agenda: motion to strike the conflict-of-interest item
chapters.summary: Kellie Okonek moved to strike item 6, the municipal attorney's briefing on January's conflict-of-interest votes, and the motion failed 3-2.
bullets: Okonek argued the board had formally closed the topic at its last meeting and should only reopen it through an ethics board review.
Mike Edgington said ignoring the municipal attorney's advice on the January actions would be a mistake.
Jennifer Wingard objected that the questions put to the attorney were asked privately by the chair, not through the board.
Bryan Burnett asked whether the briefing would settle the matter once and for all; the chair said he hoped so.

chapters.title: Agenda amendment and approval of minutes
chapters.summary: The board added a letter on the wildfire protection plan's hazard rating to new business, approved the amended agenda, and approved the February 23 and March 5 minutes.
bullets: The added item questions the Community Wildfire Protection Plan's hazard rating for Girdwood, which was based on Anchorage weather data.

chapters.title: Presentation: Girdwood Parks Master Plan public draft
chapters.summary: Bray Keefer of Huddle AK presented the public review draft of the Girdwood Parks Master Plan, which is open for comment until April 5.
bullets: The plan updates a 1985 parks plan and covers Moose Meadows, Town Square, Girdwood Park, Lions Club Park and the greenbelt.
The process included site inventories, a community survey with over 200 responses, two public meetings and an advisory group.
It proposes future parkland, including a Glacier Creek Park south of Girdwood Park and two areas north of the airport now managed by HLB.
After revisions it goes to the Planning and Zoning Commission at the end of April, with a public hearing in early June.
Comments can be submitted through the form at girdwoodparksplan.com.

chapters.title: Parks Master Plan: questions on commenting and costs
chapters.summary: Supervisors asked how public comments will be tracked and whether the plan estimates costs; it doesn't, and projects will be prioritized and costed later.
bullets: People can submit several comments at different times; an email address is requested so the consultants can follow up.
Comments don't need to be formally substantive, and they will be categorized in a spreadsheet and summarized in an appendix.
The plan only goes to Planning and Zoning and doesn't become part of the comprehensive plan.
Kyle Kelly said each project would get a feasibility study and cost estimate once the board sets priorities.

chapters.title: Legislative report: Senator Cathy Giessel
chapters.summary: Senator Cathy Giessel reported on an elections bill and on the Senate Resources Committee's skeptical review of the governor's gas pipeline property tax bill.
bullets: The elections bill drops the envelope signature requirement for mail ballots, lets voters correct ballot errors, and pays return postage.
The governor's bill would bar local property taxes on the pipeline from the start of construction until gas flow reaches one billion cubic feet a day.
It would replace the 20-mill property tax with a volumetric tax of six cents per thousand cubic feet, collected by the state.
Giessel said the committee won't rush, since projections suggest the gas would cost more than Cook Inlet gas does today.
Asked about high oil prices, she estimated about $500 million in extra state revenue if prices hold through June.

chapters.title: Legislative report: Representative Ky Holland
chapters.summary: Representative Ky Holland reported that the elections bill passed the House and gave updates on the budget and several bills affecting Girdwood.
bullets: The draft budget adds education funding, fully funds expected wildfire and disaster costs, and puts some money in the statutory budget reserve.
The Whittier railroad land transfer bill reached the House floor, with final passage expected Wednesday.
House Bill 346 on airport buffers near housing and House Bill 317 on rights-of-way for wildfire safety on single-access roads are both getting hearings.
Holland and Senator Giessel plan a town hall on April 18 at 11 a.m., and Chugach Electric holds a town hall tomorrow at 6 p.m.

chapters.title: Assembly, school board and HOBAC reports
chapters.summary: No Assembly member, school board member or HOBAC representative was present yet, so the board moved on to supervisor reports.

chapters.title: Supervisor reports: highway speed limit and bed tax
chapters.summary: Kellie Okonek reported that DOT is moving to lower the Alyeska Highway speed limit, and the board added the topic to old business.
bullets: A departing DOT official requested the speed limit change, but it's unclear whether the safety countermeasures the study called for will follow.
The Public Safety Advisory Committee suggested a public hearing; supervisors debated whether that belongs at the Land Use Committee.
Kyle Kelly offered to brief the board on the speed study when the item comes up.
The chair reported the Municipality is directing tourism improvement funds from bed tax revenue to downtown projects and marketing, and wants that on a future agenda.

chapters.title: Supervisor reports: tsunami signs and wildfire preparedness
chapters.summary: Brianna Sullivan reported on tsunami evacuation signs, a proposed wildland-urban interface service area, and plans to hand out wildfire sprinkler kits.
bullets: The Office of Emergency Management is ready to install tsunami evacuation signs in Girdwood but needs about $15,000.
An April 14 Assembly resolution, worked on with Zach Johnson, asks the administration to explore a wildland-urban interface service area.
Anchorage's wildfire division runs out of funding in a year, so the work needs to start now.
Residents explained the sprinkler kits: tripod sprinklers plus a hose that connects to firefighters' water tanks, distributed to homes at events like Forest Fair.

chapters.title: Committee updates and standing reports
chapters.summary: The chair ran through committee updates and standing reports, highlighting that short-term rental registration starts around May 1.
bullets: GHEC's two agenda items tonight are the housing RFP and its member vacancies.
Parcel H has no new activity while a legal case continues in the courts.
Short-term rental operators will have a 90-day window to register under the new municipal regulations.

chapters.title: Fire department report
chapters.summary: Kyle Kelly gave the fire department's report: six new firefighters, new equipment and grants, and a weekend avalanche rescue.
bullets: Six new firefighters started March 21, and the department is training for wildfire season.
A new tracked Polaris Ranger arrived, and a grant will add a skid pump for quick wildland response.
The department responded with Chugach Powder Guides to an avalanche that caught recreational skiers.
A new engine for Girdwood passed factory inspection and should arrive by June.

chapters.title: Police report and police IT levy
chapters.summary: Kyle Kelly gave the Whittier police report, and the board discussed whether the police IT levy could buy equipment for Girdwood's contracted department.
bullets: The department has two open positions, with one job offer out to a candidate who would attend the academy in Fairbanks.
It is applying for grants to replace a radio system that will lose support.
Equipment bought with the levy would have to be municipally owned and loaned to the department, not spent on services.

chapters.title: Parks and trails report
chapters.summary: Kyle Kelly reported on icy, soft spring trails, returning seasonal staff, and new bridge and picnic pavilion projects.
bullets: Trails are icy and soft; people should let them dry out and read avalanche advisories.
Seasonal staff return in mid-April, and the department is looking for a volunteer campground host.
Lumber has arrived to replace a footbridge near Town Square, paid for with help from a private donor.
A new picnic pavilion at Lions Club Park, funded by a grant and $5,000 from the Lions Club, will be built in May.
Staff are applying for a Parks Foundation grant for interpretive signs about the hand tram and the historic mining district.

chapters.title: Roads report: overflow, steaming and breakup
chapters.summary: Kyle Kelly described constant steaming and grading to keep overflow off Girdwood's roads, and preparations for spring breakup.
bullets: Crews steamed six of seven days last week to keep creeks in their culverts.
Last Friday overflow sent a creek down a road toward a home before the steam truck cleared it.
Crews are pushing back berms and bringing in a blower to widen roads before breakup.

chapters.title: Roads report: fish passage design and bridge bid
chapters.summary: Kyle Kelly reported that the fish passage culvert design is waiting on an RFP, and that the bridge bid came in at the engineer's estimate.
bullets: The EPA approved the RFP language, and the culvert design is waiting on municipal purchasing to assign a buyer.
The winning bridge bid, from Spurnack and Sons, came in at about $2.9 million, close to the six-month-old engineer's estimate.
A lower bid from an Idaho contractor was disqualified for lacking Alaska qualifications.
Dirt work may start this summer, depending on when the steel arrives and how the contractor schedules it.

chapters.title: Roads report: maintenance contract and winter costs
chapters.summary: Kyle Kelly explained the delayed road maintenance contract bid and a very expensive January, which will likely mean less summer work.
bullets: Purchasing questioned how the contract mixes maintenance with Davis-Bacon construction work; after a meeting it accepted the approach.
The current contract will be extended two months so a new five-year contract can be bid.
January's invoice was unusually large because of ice, steaming, excavation and sanding after a mid-winter warm-up.
Larger bidders came in near $4 million on the bridge, which Kelly said is typical for firms built for state megaprojects.
Kelly said this winter needed more steaming than his previous 14 years combined, so next year he'll keep a backup steam truck contract on call.

chapters.title: Library report
chapters.summary: The board heard about upcoming library events and the April library fundraiser.
bullets: Events include a haiku contest through April, a poetry tea on the 11th, and a recipe swap on the 18th.

chapters.title: Public comment
chapters.summary: Candidates for the Board of Supervisors, including Nick Crews, introduced themselves, a Chugach Electric advisory council member invited residents to tomorrow's town hall, and a resident thanked organizers of Saturday's candidate debate.
bullets: Amanda Tuttle announced a Wednesday meet-and-greet for her Seat D campaign, and another candidate reminded voters to return ballots by April 7.
Nick Crews, a software engineer who grew up in Girdwood, named housing, land use, and the relationship with the Municipality as his priorities.
The Chugach Electric town hall will cover natural gas imports, renewables, and pressure to join the gas line project.
The board asked staff to link the debate recording in the minutes.

chapters.title: School board report: bond and levy
chapters.summary: School board member Andy Holleman explained the one-time school levy and the bond package on the municipal ballot.
bullets: Higher property values opened room under the state's equity formula to send more local money to the district, but doing so hits the tax cap and needs voter approval.
The levy is one-time and won't recur without another vote.
The bond would upgrade Lake Otis school and renovate Romig Middle School; nothing in it is specific to Girdwood.

chapters.title: Assembly report: Zach Johnson
chapters.summary: Assembly member Zach Johnson reported on recent and upcoming Assembly actions, from natural gas supply and animal neglect to data centers and a rewrite of the building code.
bullets: The Assembly adopted a resolution recognizing the need for new natural gas supply, and updated code on animal neglect.
Upcoming: zoning rules for data centers, the school district budget, and a 250-page rewrite of Title 23, the building code.
A resolution would reallocate $700,000 in HUD funds to a housing rehabilitation program.
Johnson expects a vote tomorrow on allowing food production as an accessory use, and offered to help draft a Girdwood version.
The chair noted that the building code applies in Girdwood but isn't enforced by the Municipality there.

chapters.title: Municipal attorney on the January conflict-of-interest vote
chapters.summary: Assistant Municipal Attorney Zach Schwartz said municipal code doesn't treat holding two municipal roles as a conflict of interest, and the board then voted 3-2 to vacate its January vote.
bullets: The board limited the item to 15 minutes.
Schwartz said code addresses conflicts between private interests and official duties, not between two official roles, and that the Board of Ethics has the final say.
He compared it to Assembly members, who don't recuse themselves from voting for their own chair.
Kellie Okonek argued that any challenge should go through the Board of Ethics rather than be decided in 15 minutes.
Bryan Burnett, absent in January, was reluctant to vote on it.

chapters.title: Dispute over what the vacate vote meant
chapters.summary: Supervisors disagreed about which January vote had been vacated, and a motion to reconsider was ruled out of order because it didn't come from the prevailing side.
bullets: Okonek said the chair had been recused in January and that the conflict still stood.
The chair offered a separate motion to send the question to the Board of Ethics.
Jennifer Wingard challenged the chair's ruling to ask what exactly had been voted on.
Staff restated the motion as vacating the January vote that was based on the conflict of interest.

chapters.title: Food production as an accessory use: postponed to April
chapters.summary: The board postponed to April whether to support an Assembly ordinance allowing small-scale food production as an accessory use, which can't simply be extended to Girdwood.
bullets: Girdwood's code allows cottage crafts only in commercial zones, so the Anchorage ordinance has no Girdwood equivalent.
Options include a resolution supporting it in principle, folding it into the Girdwood land use code rewrite, or sending it back to committee.
Supervisors wanted to see what the Assembly passes tomorrow before acting.

chapters.title: Housing action plan RFP approved
chapters.summary: The board voted 5-0 to issue an RFP for a housing action and implementation plan, not to exceed $100,000 from the GHEC budget.
bullets: Brooks Chandler said the RFP follows the comprehensive plan's call for a housing strategy and a housing action plan.
It asks the consultant to estimate costs and funding for specific strategies, avoiding a plan that only calls for more plans.
A resident noted it also asks whether dense housing is economically feasible on specific HLB properties.
Staff will route the RFP through municipal purchasing, using the parks plan RFP as a template.
A supervisor asked GHEC to find comparison communities closer to Girdwood's situation than Whitefish or Breckenridge.

chapters.title: Parliamentary procedure training approved
chapters.summary: The board approved, by consent, up to $275 for a parliamentary procedure training for the incoming board, open to the whole community.
bullets: The trainer, who led the training at the community council summit, quoted $250 for an hour plus Q&A in Girdwood.
It will be scheduled after the new board is seated.
Ethics and effective-meeting trainings through the Alaska Municipal League are also being considered.

chapters.title: Resolution supporting the hand tram interpretive signs grant
chapters.summary: The board voted 5-0 for a resolution supporting the Girdwood Trails Committee's Anchorage Park Foundation grant application for interpretive signs at the new bridge.
bullets: The plans include an interpretive area, a tram car on display, and signs on the mine side of the bridge.
The grant would match $15,000 from the Park Foundation with $15,000 in-kind from the Trails Committee.
It is a two-year grant, so the signs can be built whenever the bridge construction allows.

chapters.title: GHEC vacancies
chapters.summary: With no applicants for GHEC's two open seats, the board kept recruiting through its notices and dropped the item from the agenda until GHEC asks for action.
bullets: GHEC is down from seven members to five but has had no trouble making quorum.
GHEC preferred not to shrink to five members yet.
Openings will be advertised in the board's regular notices rather than through general outreach.

chapters.title: Alyeska Highway speed limit: joint meeting with DOT
chapters.summary: The board agreed by consent to hold a joint GBOS and Land Use Committee community meeting with DOT on the proposed Alyeska Highway speed limit cut.
bullets: Kyle Kelly said the departing DOT official ordered the limit lowered from 45 to 40 mph without the engineering measures the speed study recommended.
Without those measures, enforcement would fall on Girdwood's small police department.
Kellie Okonek relayed DOT's view that a limit below the road's natural driving speed can make it less safe.
Supervisors favored radar feedback signs, possibly a portable one, as a more achievable first step.
Kelly will ask DOT to send someone to the joint meeting.

chapters.title: Parks Master Plan resolution: April or May
chapters.summary: Staff said a resolution supporting the final Parks Master Plan will come to the board in April or May, before it goes to Planning and Zoning.

chapters.title: GBOS rules and procedures: another work session
chapters.summary: The board reviewed draft revisions to its rules and procedures and agreed to hold another work session in May, after the new board is seated.
bullets: The draft fixes things that are out of date with code, such as references to the cemetery board.
Open questions include term limits and stricter adherence to Robert's Rules to shorten meetings.
Supervisors debated fixing known errors now versus finishing one full revision, then chose a single revision.
The work session's recommendation would start the required 60-day review.

chapters.title: Topics for the April 27 quarterly meeting with the Municipality
chapters.summary: Supervisors suggested topics for the April 27 quarterly meeting with the Municipality, including tourism improvement projects and a parks surcharge.
bullets: The Anchorage parks and recreation surcharge, carried over from last time.
How bed tax revenue is spent on tourism improvement projects.
Follow-ups on IGC, including keeping a community-started project from being handed to a developer.

chapters.title: Wildfire protection plan hazard rating letter
chapters.summary: Mike Edgington and Brianna Sullivan will review the final Community Wildfire Protection Plan and bring a letter or resolution on Girdwood's high hazard rating to the next meeting.
bullets: The board's comment that Girdwood's rating relied on Anchorage weather data got no direct response before the plan passed.
The high rating is starting to affect insurance rates.
The project manager said every comment was reviewed and changes went into the final draft, without individual replies.
The board may invite her to the next meeting.

chapters.title: Adjournment
chapters.summary: The meeting adjourned.
